source: The Made Real Blueprint - Step 1 Picture workbook v19.docx (September 2026)
source_note: The workbook's opening line 'You have read the Introduction' is left out in the app: the Introduction is a separate document and is not part of the app.

schema_notes.ids: Part, exercise, summary and field IDs are stable keys for saved answers. Do not rename them when only the wording changes.
schema_notes.text: 'intro' and 'prompt' may be a string or a list of paragraphs. 'intro_title' is the heading above a part's explanation. An exercise 'promise' is the one line under its title. 'bullets' is a bullet list shown after the prompt. A field 'hint' is a short text shown above that field; 'heading' starts a new block inside the exercise. A field 'marker' (A, B, C…) is shown as a large letter before its label.
schema_notes.optional: 'optional': true marks a part or exercise the person may skip.
schema_notes.summary: Each part (except Part 5) ends with a 'summary' block ('What does this tell me?'). The person fills it in; the AI partner may offer a draft from their own answers. 'result' is the one-line result of the part.
schema_notes.unknown_numbers: Number and money cells accept 'unknown' or '?'. A total with an unknown number is shown as not complete yet — an unknown never counts as zero.
schema_notes.story_status: 'draft' = Mwata still checks the wording and facts. 'ready' = checked.
schema_notes.boxes: 'tips' = a 'Good to know' box. 'watch_out' = a 'Watch out' box. 'challenge' = 'A friendly challenge'. 'story' = 'My story — Mwata' (a 'go_deeper' block may hold its own story). 'talk' (on a part) = 'Talk about it'. 'result_guide' = 'What your result means'. 'example_page' = a fully filled-in example, shown as rows.
schema_notes.tables: 'tables' on an exercise are fixed content tables (not filled in): 'place' ('before' or 'after' the answer fields), 'lead' above it, optional 'header' row, and 'after' below it.

field_types.long_text: Free text area. 'lines' is a hint for the height; 'placeholder' is grey ghost text that is never saved.
field_types.list: A fixed number of short text items ('count').
field_types.table: Rows x columns. 'row_labels' are fixed labels in the first column ('row_header' is its title; 'row_labels_editable' says which of them the person may rewrite); if 'rows' is given without labels, rows are empty. 'rows_from' fills the rows from another answer. 'columns' lists the columns the user fills in; column 'kind' is text, long_text, number, money or choice (with 'options'). 'column_names_from' renames the columns after another answer. 'totals': true shows totals for money columns ('totals_label'); 'total_filter' counts only rows whose column value is in the list; 'extra_totals' adds further total rows with their own filter.
field_types.checkbox_pick: Pick from 'options'. 'pick' = how many to choose (no 'pick' = any number). 'allow_custom' = user may add own words.
field_types.yes_no: One answer per item in 'questions'. 'options' lists the answers (default: Yes, No).
field_types.calculation: A worked calculation with an 'Example' column (fixed text) and a 'Me' column. Each row is an input, comes 'from' a table total in another exercise, or is a 'formula' of earlier row IDs in the same exercise. 'condition' shows a row only when it is true. 'format' (money by default): 'left_or_short' or 'months'.
field_types.image_board: Pictures the person adds (a vision board), up to 'max'. Each picture has a one-line caption ('caption_label'). The pictures stay in the person's own account; the AI partner reads only the captions.

step.title: Picture
step.question: What life do I really want?
tagline: Now the real work begins, and it begins with you.
intro: In this first step, you build a clearer picture of the life you want. You look honestly at where you stand today, including your money. You finish with a Working Direction: what you want to explore next. This is not a final decision. That comes in Step 3, after you have explored your options.

Every exercise starts with a short explanation, then asks you to apply it to your own life. I give you the tools and questions, and share my own story, including the parts that changed along the way. You do the work of deciding what fits you.

ways_to_use.title: Three ways to use this step
rows: Read, think, write. Print it and use a pen, or type in the boxes. Everything you need is in here. Nothing else is required.
Each part has a short video where I explain the same ideas in my own words. Watch first, then answer the questions.
The same questions in digital form, with an AI partner that remembers your answers and asks about them later. Useful if you prefer typing to paper.

how_it_works.title: How this step works
bullets: Two ways to start. The First Picture takes about 20–30 minutes and gives you a first summary today. The full Picture step has 5 parts and takes a few hours in total. Spread it over two weeks, or work at a pace that suits you.

Short on time? Follow the core path: the First Picture, 1.1, 1.2, 1.4, 2.1, 3.2 to 3.5, 4.1, 4.2 and Part 5. That gives you a complete Working Direction. The other exercises help you explore it further.
Every exercise follows the same pattern. First the explanation, then "Now you". Some exercises include an optional "Go deeper" section. Use it when you have the time and energy.
The people in the examples are made up. They show what an answer can look like. Your answers can be completely different.
There are no perfect answers. "I don't know yet" is an honest answer. Write it down, along with how you could find out.
Write in your own language if you prefer.
Each part ends with "What does this tell me?" Use your answers to complete a short summary.
"Talk about it" boxes help you discuss your plans with your partner, family, friends, people in the network, or me.

word_help.title: Word help
items: something your new life really needs.
something you will not accept, even if everything else is good.
money you keep aside for emergencies, not for everyday spending.
getting one thing by giving up another.
what you want to explore next, not a final decision.

tips: Stuck on a question? Skip it and come back later. The answer often comes while you walk, cook or shower.

parts.promise: Four questions. About 20 minutes. A first picture of what you want.
parts.intro: Start here if you want a first picture today. These four questions give you something useful to work with before you explore it further in the full workbook.
parts.route_title: Your First Picture, a quick way in

finish.title: My First Picture
finish.description: A first picture of what you want.

fields.label: One moment that felt good
fields.hint: Think of one moment in the last few years when you felt content, engaged or proud. What happened? What made it possible?

fields.label: A normal day
fields.hint: Imagine a normal day in the life you want. Not a holiday. Write five sentences, from morning to evening.

fields.label: What you want to keep
fields.hint: What is good in your life now that you want to keep, wherever you live?

fields.label: Your biggest question
fields.hint: What is the biggest question you have about your future right now?

summary.title: My First Picture
summary.prompt: Look at your four answers. Then finish these sentences.

fields.label: What I want more of
What I want to keep
What matters to me in daily life
Something that pulls in two directions
My one small action this week
Something I want to test later, and what it would help me learn

tips: Look for wishes that pull in two directions. For example: "I want quiet, but I also want friends close by." That is useful information. You can choose one for now, combine both (a quiet home fifteen minutes from a village), or put them in order: first this, later that. If you have not noticed a tension, write "none noticed yet". You do not need to invent a problem.

example.text: More of: time outside and control over my week. Keep: weekly dinners with my sister. Daily life: calm mornings and meaningful work. Two directions: I want to live in the countryside, but I love being close to my family. Action this week: ask my manager if I can work from another place two days a week.

summary.closing: Continue with Part 1 when you are ready. If you have completed the First Picture, bring your answers with you. Add to them or change them where it helps.

parts.label: Part 1
parts.title: Picture your new life
parts.promise: Most people know exactly what they do not want. Now we find out what you really want.
intro: A big life change often starts with "Where shall I go?" or "Can I afford it?" Both questions matter. Here, we begin with the life you want, then look at the place and the money.

You need something to judge a place or a price against. If you do not know how you want to live, every country looks good in the photos and every price looks high. Your picture is the measuring stick: it gives you a way to compare your options.

A picture goes further than a wish. A wish is a word; a picture is a scene. Two people who want "more freedom" can mean completely different things. "I decide what I do on a Tuesday morning" gives you something concrete. You can compare a job, a house or a country with it and ask: would this give me that Tuesday morning?

You are also allowed to want something ordinary. Your picture does not have to impress anyone. Mine was simple: land, my hands in the soil, a warm climate, and work that meant something. It took years to build. It never became more impressive. It became more real.
parts.intro_title: Why we start with a picture
tips: You do not need the whole picture. You need enough of it to take the next step. The rest becomes clear after that.
parts.talk: Share your normal day with your partner or a close friend. Ask: "Do you see me in this picture? What surprises you?" If you are planning this life together, each of you should write your own normal day first. Then compare and talk about where your pictures differ.

finish.title: My Life Picture
finish.description: What you want more of, what you keep, what is essential, and what is still open.

exercises.title: From "no" to "yes"
intro: Most people find "no" easier than "yes". So we start there, and then turn it around.

A "no" tells you what to leave behind. "No more long evenings at my laptop" is a useful starting point, but it does not tell you what you want to do with those evenings. For each "no", write a "yes": what you would actually do instead.
Give yourself five minutes. Write what comes to mind before you start editing your answers.

start_here.prompt: Write five things you no longer want in your life. Then, for each one, write what you want instead. Make it as concrete as you can.

example.text: No more: evenings on my laptop. Instead: I finish work at six and spend some time outside before dinner. No more: grey winters that last half a year. Instead: I can sit outside in March with a coffee.

tips: Some things you do not want have no clear "yes" yet. Write "not sure yet". You come back to them in 1.2, when you describe your normal day.

exercises.title: Moments that felt good
exercises.promise: "What is your passion?" is a hard question. "When did you feel good?" is much easier. And the answers tell you more.
intro: When someone asks what you really want, it can be hard to answer. It is a big question, and "I don't know" is often the honest response. So we start with something easier to recall.

Look at moments in your own life when things felt right. You do not have to invent them or borrow them from someone else's life online. They are real experiences, and they tell you something about what matters to you.

tables.lead: Three things are worth looking for in every good moment:
rows: Building something, teaching someone, being outside
Who was with you, or were you alone?
Alone, with one person, in a group
tables.after: The third one matters most. The activity may not be possible in your new life. The need comes with you wherever you go.

watch_out: Holidays often come to mind first because they are easy to remember. They can show you something real about yourself, but they also show what you needed a break from. That is not always the same as what you want in daily life. Include one holiday if you like, and at least one ordinary day too.

start_here.prompt: Think of three moments from the last few years when you felt content, engaged or proud. Choose at least one from an ordinary day. Where were you? What were you doing? Who was with you?

fields.hint: Look at each moment more closely. What made it possible, and what do the three moments have in common?

example.text: Sailing with my brother last summer. Repairing the old bench in the garden. Sunday breakfast with my grandchildren. What made them possible: free time, no rush. What they have in common: I was fully present, not busy with work or my phone.

story.text: I found questions like "What is your passion?" and "What makes you truly happy?" surprisingly hard. Sometimes I felt frustrated that I could not answer. What helped was remembering moments when I was building something with my hands, helping someone move forward, or spending time in nature in a warm climate. I started to see what those moments had in common. The answers were already in my life; I only had to look.

exercises.title: A normal day in your new life
exercises.promise: Not a holiday. A normal Tuesday. Because most days are normal days.
intro: Now you turn those ingredients into a day.

We use an ordinary day because that is what most of your life will be. It can feel less exciting than imagining a big change, but it gives you a useful question: would I enjoy the everyday life that comes with it?
An ordinary day also gives you something to test. You can visit a place and try living a normal Tuesday there. It is much harder to test a word like "happiness".

tables.lead: How much detail? Enough that someone else could film it. Look at the difference:
rows: "Coffee on the terrace, looking at olive trees, before anyone else is awake"
"Two mornings a week helping new business owners solve problems I understand"
"My sister can come for dinner without booking a flight"
tables.after: The detail in the right-hand column gives you something you can check against a real house, job or town.

start_here.prompt: Describe this day from morning to evening. Include an ordinary detail you would not put in a holiday brochure: housework, rain, or an hour when nothing much happens. Use these questions to help you:
bullets: Where do you wake up? What do you see from your window?
What do you do in the morning? And in the afternoon?
What is your work, or how do you spend your time?
Who is with you? How does the day end?

fields.label: The need behind the picture.
fields.hint: Olive trees might mean calm, nature or space. What are the two or three needs behind your normal day?

example.text: I wake up at 7, without an alarm. From my window, I see olive trees. I drink coffee outside. In the morning, I work four hours online for my clients. In the afternoon, I work in the garden or go to the market in the village. My partner and I cook together. Twice a week, friends come for dinner. Two afternoons a week are for paperwork and cleaning, and I don't enjoy them. I go to bed tired, but happy.

prompt: Read your day again and underline the concrete details: coffee, terrace, olive trees, clients, sister. If there are only a few, add enough detail for someone else to picture the day as clearly as you do.

Then add the less enjoyable parts: housework, paid work, a tired day, a rainy winter week, time alone. Does the picture still feel good? Could you meet the same needs another way, including closer to home?

fields.label: Make it visible
fields.hint: Collect five to eight photos of ordinary scenes that fit your day: a kitchen table, a path, a workshop, a market. Use your own photos where you can. Under each one, write the need it represents. These pictures will help you compare real places with the daily life you want.

watch_out: Some of what comes up will not be yours. It will be a life you have seen online. That is normal, and exercise 1.5 helps you spot it. For now, write everything down. You sort it later.

exercises.title: If money were no worry
exercises.promise: Time to play. For a moment, forget what seems possible.
intro: Money can limit what you allow yourself to want before you have even put it into words. It is easy to dismiss an idea as too expensive without looking at what draws you to it.
You may have done this while describing your normal day in 1.2. For this exercise, set that limit aside.
Give yourself room to describe what you want. Then bring money back into the picture and ask: what is the smallest first step towards this, and what does it cost?

Most directions have a small, inexpensive first step. You can compare countries or talk to someone who has made a similar change without spending money. Testing a business idea at a local market takes a weekend, plus the cost of stock and a stall. You do not have to start with the most expensive version.

start_here.prompt: Imagine your essential costs are covered for the rest of your life. How would you spend your time? What would you stop doing? What would you start?

fields.hint: Want to think bigger? Imagine you receive two million euros tomorrow. What would you do with it? Add it above. Then write the three answers that matter most to you.

example.text: I would bake every day and teach others. I would spend more time with my mother. I would stop my office job. With two million: a small house with a big kitchen. The three that matter most: my own bakery, time with my mother, the house.

go_deeper.prompt: Look at your three answers. Which of them really need a lot of money? Which could start much smaller, maybe this year?

story.text: In 2023, while I was living in Bali, I answered the two-million question: what would you do with two million euros? My answer was clear: buy land in Portugal and build a self-sufficient life. I did not have two million euros, but I realised I did not need that much to begin. My first step cost nothing. I listed what that life needed and compared countries against it. You will see how in Step 2. In April 2024, I travelled to Portugal to see it for myself. The land was officially mine in August 2024. Today, I am building the life I pictured.

exercises.title: What matters most
exercises.promise: Your values shape your choices, including the ones you make without thinking.
intro: You use your values every day. They influence which job you accept and why a place can feel wrong even when it looks perfect on paper. Naming them helps you understand those reactions and use them when comparing options.

tables.lead: Here, you turn what matters to you into practical criteria for your choices. Sort them into three groups:
rows: Your life needs this. Without it, the whole option is wrong, even when everything else is good.
You want it and will work for it. You could live without it for a while.
You will not accept this. It ends the discussion.
tables.after: It is easy to label everything essential. A list of ten must-haves can leave you with no workable option. In my experience, there are usually two or three that matter most. Some situations need more: health, caring for someone, or access to a school can each be essential.

start_here.prompt: Tick the five words that matter most to you. Missing a word? Write it in an empty box.

fields.hint: Choose your two most important words. What would more room for each one look like in a normal week?

columns.label: What it looks like in a normal week

fields.hint: Now make it concrete. For each must-have, ask: would I say no to a place that has everything else, but not this? Then it is essential. If not, it is strongly preferred.

columns.label: Which of these are essential, and which are strongly preferred?

fields.label: My dealbreakers
fields.hint: Things I will not accept

fields.label: What I want to keep
fields.hint: Good things in my life now

fields.label: What I can let go
fields.hint: Things I can live without

example.text: Words: family, security, nature, adventure, honesty. "Family" in a normal week: dinner together at least four times. Must-have: a good school close to home (essential). A garden (strongly preferred). Dealbreaker: more than one hour from a hospital. Keep: my weekly football team. Let go: a big car.

tips: Choosing one thing often means giving up another. Decide which trade-offs you can accept before you have spent money or committed to a place.

exercises.title: Whose picture is this?
exercises.promise: Other people help shape your picture. This exercise asks whose influence you can see in it.
intro: Family, friends, social media and past experiences all shape what we want. That does not make a wish wrong. But it is worth checking how much of the picture feels like your own before you commit to it or sell your home.

Also ask whether you are moving towards something, away from something, or both. Wanting to leave a job that leaves you tired and empty is a valid reason for change. It tells you what needs to end, but you still need to decide what you want in its place. A move is more likely to help when you know which problem you are trying to solve.

start_here.prompt: Answer these three honestly. Write your first thought. You can always change it later.

questions: I would still want this life if nobody could see it. No photos, no social media.
I am moving towards something, not only away from something.
A good friend would say: "Yes, that fits you."

fields.hint: Whose expectations or voices do you hear in your picture? Which parts feel most like your own?

example.text: Partly. I love the idea of living abroad. But I notice that part of it comes from my friends, who all talk about it. I am not sure yet which part is really mine, and that is okay for now.

exercises.challenge: Look at the middle statement. If you answered no or not sure, write one sentence about what you are moving towards. Describe what you want, beyond the problem you want to leave. If you cannot put it into words yet, that is something useful to work on.

summary.title: What does this tell me?
summary.intro: Read through your answers, then use these questions to complete the summary below:
questions: What do I want to keep?
Which trade-off matters most to me?
summary.prompt: Now bring it together in My Life Picture. Short sentences are enough.

fields.label: Moments and needs that keep coming back
What I want more of
What I want to keep
My essential must-haves
What pulls in two directions
What I still don't know

example.text: What keeps coming back: making something with my hands, one person nearby, no rush. More of: time outside every day, work I choose, quiet mornings. Keep: Sunday dinner with my sister, my two long-standing clients, swimming twice a week. Essential: ground to grow food, internet good enough for video calls, a hospital within 45 minutes because of my mother. Pulls in two directions: quiet countryside against Sunday dinners with my sister, so for now, countryside but no more than three hours from her. Still don't know: whether my clients would stay if I moved abroad, what a house with land really costs, and how much of "abroad" is really mine.

summary.result: My Life Picture — what you want more of, what you keep, what is essential, and what is still open.

parts.label: Part 2
parts.title: Look honestly at today
parts.promise: You cannot plan a route if you do not know where you start.
intro: This part is not about judging yourself. It is about seeing clearly.

This can feel like an invitation to list everything that is wrong. In my experience, it often does the opposite. Most people I have guided found more to build on than they expected: things they had already done, people willing to help, money they had overlooked, and skills they could use in a new setting.
Your later plans depend on an honest view of where you stand now. If you guess your starting point, you guess your plan too. Give yourself the time to look carefully, without being hard on yourself.
parts.talk: Want to hear what held other people back at the start? Ask in the network, or ask someone who made a big change. You may hear some of your own beliefs, and how they found a way through them.

finish.title: My Starting Point
finish.description: Where you stand, what you can build on, and what you will check.

exercises.title: Your life today, and in one year
exercises.promise: A simple picture of how your life is doing, area by area.
intro: This exercise uses the wheel of life, a tool coaches have used for decades. You score each area of your life to see the whole picture, rather than letting one problem dominate it.

It helps in two ways. First, it separates things that can get mixed together. "I am unhappy" becomes "my work is fine, but my free time feels empty". Second, comparing today with where you want to be in one year shows which gaps matter to you. A 5 you are happy with needs no action. A 7 you want to bring up to 9 deserves your attention.
The score is only a starting point. The explanation beside it is what makes it useful.
tips: A number shows how you feel, not what to do. Next to each score, write what it looks like in real life. Not "work: 9", but "work: 9, I finish in time to eat with my family." That sentence tells you what to protect when your life changes.

start_here.prompt: Score each area from 1 (very unhappy) to 10 (very happy), first for today and then for where you would like to be in one year. Write "n/a" for anything that does not apply. Describe what today's score looks like in a normal week, and what would be different in a year.

columns.label: What my score looks like in a normal week

fields.heading: Then look at your time
fields.hint: The wheel shows how you feel. Your week shows how you spend your time. Think of a normal week and estimate the hours. Rough numbers are fine.
row_labels: Home, chores and care for others
Things I do just for me

fields.hint: Which one change would give you the most time back? Does it need a new country, or could it start next month?

example.text: Work and travel: 50 hours now, 38 wanted. Screens without a purpose: 12 now, 5 wanted. Outside: 2 now, 8 wanted. The biggest change is my commute, eight hours a week. That does not need a new country. It needs a conversation with my manager.

go_deeper.prompt: Which area has the biggest gap? Which area pulls you most towards a change, and which one makes a change most difficult?

story.text: I first used the wheel of life after a year in Bali. Work was going well, and I gave home and surroundings a 9. My relationship and personal growth each scored 5. That helped me decide where to focus and write down a few actions. I have done the exercise every year since. It is encouraging to see the difference: personal growth went from 5 to 8. But the wheel also showed me that a good score can change. As Bali became busier, with more buildings, traffic and pollution, my score for home and surroundings fell from 9 to 6. I had to ask myself whether Bali was still the home I wanted.

exercises.title: What you have already done
exercises.promise: Before we look at what is difficult, look at what you have already achieved.
intro: When you imagine a big change, it is easy to forget the difficult things you have already managed. That can leave you thinking: "I could never do that."

Think about how you managed those difficult things. If you moved house on your own while working, you learned to break a big task into steps. If you cared for a parent, you learned how to keep going when someone depended on you. Those experiences can help you work out how to approach a new challenge.

start_here.prompt: Think of three things you are proud of. How did you manage each one? Which strengths or support could you draw on again?

columns.label: Strength or support I can use again

example.text: I raised two children alone while working full-time. I learned to drive at 40. I organised care for my father. How: step by step, and I asked for help. I can use again: patience, making lists, and my sister's support.

tips: Look at the last column. Not everything transfers to a new situation. But usually more than you think.

story.text: Alongside my consultancy work, I missed doing something connected to building, which has always interested me. When I bought a newly built house in Bali, I wanted an inspector for extra reassurance, even though I could check it myself. Finding a good one proved difficult, and that gave me an idea. I took an online course and became an accredited inspector with InterNACHI. The course took about half a year. Including a simple website and an Instagram page, I invested about €2,000. The rest was my time. Promoting myself was the hardest part. I have always been more comfortable showing what I can do than selling it. Two months after putting the company online and introducing it to several agents, I had my first client. The work came through a recommendation from the estate agent who had handled my own purchase. That was how the business started. It taught me to pay attention to frustrations that could become opportunities, and to the people who already trusted my work.

go_deeper.title: Connect the dots
go_deeper.prompt: Look back at your life and mark three turning points: a move, a choice, a person, a setback. What did each one lead to? As Steve Jobs said, you can only connect the dots looking backwards. Together, those moments can show a pattern: a need you keep returning to, a skill you keep using, or a kind of place that keeps drawing you.

fields.hint: What connects all three? Does it point in the same direction as your Life Picture?

story.text: When I was 21, shortly after graduating from technical college (HTS), I moved to Thailand with my parents. The move was their decision, but I was closely involved in finding land, building our home, and settling into a place where we had a new language to learn. Asia felt like home. I returned to the Netherlands for my career, but I already knew I would not stay there forever. Another connection was my interest in technology and building, which started when I was young. It runs through my engineering career, the inspection business in Bali, and the land in Portugal. Looking back helped me see how those experiences fitted together.

exercises.title: What stopped you before?
exercises.promise: Earlier attempts are not failures. They are information.
intro: Most of us have tried to change something before: a plan we never started, a move we postponed, or a business that remained an idea. Look at what stopped you and sort it into three groups.
Outside your control: rules changing, illness, a pandemic. You cannot prevent these. You can plan for them, with a reserve, a fallback, or a slower timeline.
Things you can partly influence: money, work, health, and the people around you. You do not decide these alone, but what you do changes them over time.

Inside your control: the approach you chose, the information you never gathered, the conversation you avoided, the moment you stopped asking. These are worth studying, because you can do them differently this time.
An earlier attempt can involve all three. Separating them helps you see what to prepare for, what to work on over time, and what to do differently now.

start_here.prompt: Have you tried to change your life before? What happened? Tick what fits, then write a few sentences.

options: Something outside my control (rules, illness, events)
Something I can influence over time (money, work, health, people)

fields.hint: Now the useful question: what will you do differently this time, and what will you simply plan for?

go_deeper.prompt: Look at your earlier attempts together. Is there a pattern in how they stop? For example: you start strong and stop at the first "no". Or you wait until everything is certain. A pattern you can name is a pattern you can plan for.

story.text: In 2020, I sold my house in the Netherlands to travel the world. Then COVID stopped those plans. I rented an apartment in Leiden and used the time to think. Someone gave me a book by Michael Pilarczyk, which led me to his Perfect Life programme. I started it in Leiden and continued during a two-month sabbatical in Bali at the end of 2021, when I was finding out whether that life suited me. I wrote down what I wanted: to live near the sea, in a warm climate, running my own business and helping people. It felt right. I returned to the Netherlands, left my job, and moved to Bali on my own with two bags. I could not control the interruption, but I could decide what to do with the time.

exercises.title: Beliefs I never checked
exercises.promise: We all carry beliefs we never checked. Some hold us back. Others look attractive, but may not be true either.
intro: "I am too old to start again." "Life there is cheaper." These can both feel like facts, even when we have not checked them.

The beliefs that hold us back are often easier to notice because they hurt. The appealing ones deserve just as much attention. When something supports a plan we like, we are less inclined to question it. That can become expensive later.

Often, checking a belief takes one phone call, an official website, or a conversation with someone who lives there. If you cannot check it, keep it as an uncertainty to plan for, rather than treating it as a fact.

rows: "I am too old to start again."
"A bigger garden will make me happier."
"I first need to speak the language perfectly."
"Once I move, I will feel less stressed."

start_here.prompt: Write three of your own beliefs, of either kind. How could you check if each one is true?

columns.label: Holds me back or sounds attractive?

go_deeper.prompt: Take your strongest belief. Are you 100% sure it is true? How would you act if it turned out to be false?

exercises.title: Ask people who know you
exercises.promise: Other people sometimes see things in us that we cannot see ourselves.
intro: In the 1950s, psychologists Joseph Luft and Harrington Ingham developed the Johari window. It has four areas. Here, we use the one they called the blind area: things other people notice about you that you do not see yourself. Asking for specific feedback can help you recognise them.
Ask for observations and examples. This is not a vote on your plan, and you do not need anyone's permission. A specific question gives people more to work with than a broad request for feedback.

start_here.prompt: Ask two or three people who know you well to answer in writing. A message is fine:
bullets: What am I good at?
When do you see me at my happiest?
What could hold me back?
Please give one example of something you have seen me do.

fields.hint: Then write what surprised you.

start_here.closing: No one to ask? Read old messages, cards or feedback you received. Or ask yourself: what would a good friend say?

tips: Their answers are a perspective, not a verdict. Look at the examples they give, and decide which points deserve more thought, including the uncomfortable ones.

story.text: I asked my mother and my brother to write down how they saw me. Some of what they said made me proud: that I was reliable, caring, and there when someone needed help. Other parts were harder to read. Both said, in their own words, that I sometimes reacted before really listening. I was defensive at first, but I recognised the truth in it. Since then, I have worked on listening, especially in my relationship. Exercises that help me notice my body and emotions have taught me to pause and ask: do I have room to listen properly right now? I still need to practise, but I have become much better at it. Their feedback helped me see something I had missed on my own.

summary.title: What does this tell me?
summary.intro: Read through your answers, then use these questions to complete the summary below:
questions: Which belief should I check first?
summary.prompt: Now bring it together in My Starting Point. Short sentences are enough.

fields.label: Where I stand today: my strongest and weakest areas
Where my time goes, and the change that would give me most time back
Strengths and support I can use
What stopped me before, and what I will do differently
Beliefs I will check (both kinds)
What I still don't know

summary.result: My Starting Point — where you stand, what you can build on, and what you will check.

parts.label: Part 3
parts.title: Your first money picture
parts.promise: A picture becomes a plan when you give it numbers.
parts.intro_title: Rough numbers now beat perfect numbers later.
intro: It is easy to put off the numbers, or to look once, feel overwhelmed, and stop. Start with rough figures. You will improve them as you learn more.

At this stage, the numbers help you choose a direction and a timescale. A plan that is out of reach this year could work in three years or with another source of income. Sometimes a version of your plan will not work financially. Then you need to change it, postpone it, or set it aside.
Start with three numbers:
intro_bullets: What does my new life cost per month? (3.2)
What does the change itself cost, one time? (3.3)
parts.intro_after: In 3.5 you put those three together in one simple check, with an example next to it. Mark how sure you are about every number. A figure you have checked and one you have guessed can look identical on paper. Use the same three labels throughout: known, estimate, unknown.
tips: Use an estimate if you have one, and mark it as an estimate. If you do not know, write "unknown" and how you will check. An unknown number means your total isn't complete yet. It never counts as zero.
Start with one recent bank statement and a calculator. Fill in today's costs first, because you can look those up. Leave the new-life column unknown wherever you still need information.

setup.intro: Choose one version of your new life to cost first. Keep a move to Portugal separate from a plan to work fewer hours at home. Start with the version you most want to explore. You can repeat the exercise for another version later.

fields.label: The version I am costing here
My currency
fields.app_note: Use the currency from the person's profile; changing it here updates the profile.

fields.label: Number of people in my household

parts.talk: Money is often the hardest thing to talk about. If you share your life with someone, talk about it together: what does "enough money" mean to each of you? What makes each of you feel safe? Your three words from 3.1 are a good way in. You don't need the same answer, but you need to know each other's answers.

finish.title: My First Money Picture
finish.description: Your first numbers, how sure they are, and what to check next.

exercises.title: What does money mean to you?
intro: Before you start calculating, take a minute to notice how you feel about money. Two people with the same balance can make very different choices: one sees freedom, the other worries about running out. Knowing your own response helps you understand how you read the numbers.

start_here.prompt: Write the first three words that come up when you think about money. Freedom? Worry? Safety? Stress? There is no wrong answer.

fields.hint: What would help you work through the numbers: a quiet hour, a calculator, someone beside you, or two shorter sessions? Write it down, then arrange it.

start_here.closing: Keep your three words for the summary at the end of this part. Share them with anyone you make money decisions with. If one of you thinks of fear and the other of freedom, the same numbers can feel very different.

exercises.title: What does your life cost per month, now and in your new life?
intro: Yearly costs are easy to miss when you think in months: insurance, car repairs, gifts, a holiday, the dentist. Divide them by twelve and include them in the table, unless you have already counted them elsewhere. For example, 1,200 a year for insurance, repairs and gifts adds 100 a month.

start_here.prompt: Write the costs per month. In the last column, mark each new-life number: known, estimate or unknown.

row_labels: Care costs (children, or someone you care for)
Yearly costs not already above, divided by 12 (gifts, holidays, repairs)
fields.totals_label: Total per month (you use this in 3.5)

example.text: A normal month in a small rented house in the interior of central Portugal, 2026. Rent €550. Energy €200, more in winter. Water and waste €30. Food €450, including one meal out a week. Car, fuel and insurance €250. Private health insurance 2 × €60. Phone and internet €35. Free time €150. Flights to visit family €100. Yearly costs divided by 12: €100. Total: about €2,000 a month. Rent is an estimate; energy, food, fuel, internet and health insurance are close to what people here really pay.

exercises.title: What does the change itself cost, one time?
intro: These are the costs you pay once to make the change. Include them early: a monthly budget can work on paper while the initial costs leave you short in month two.

start_here.prompt: Only write money you will really spend.

row_labels: Paying for two homes for a while (if this happens)
fields.totals_label: Total one-time cost (you use this in 3.5)

tips: Deposits, for example, for a rental home, are not in this list. You usually get them back later, but you cannot use that money for a while. You subtract them in 3.5.

exercises.title: What comes in per month?
intro: Separate income you can count on from income you hope to earn. A potential client and an existing salary can look much the same in a budget. Only confirmed income goes into the check in 3.5. Record agreed income separately, with the month it starts, so you can see it without counting on it yet.

rows: You have evidence it continues in the new situation. For example, a contract that allows you to work from abroad.
Promised, but not started yet. A client said yes; work begins next year.
An idea. It may well happen, but nothing supports it yet.

start_here.prompt: List your current income sources and those you expect in your new life. Use income after tax and other deductions. If you do not know your future take-home pay, write "unknown" in the new-life column and note the gross amount alongside it for later. Keep gross amounts out of the confirmed total: they are not what reaches your account. You will work through tax in Step 3 with a professional.

extra_totals.label: Total agreed (not in the check yet)

example.text: Now: salary as a graphic designer. In my new life: that salary stops; my employer won't let me work from abroad. Freelance work for two current clients (agreed), renting out a room (hoped), design workshops later (hoped).

exercises.title: A first money check
exercises.promise: Two simple questions: do I have money left each month, and if not, how long do my savings cover the gap?
intro: The second number is your runway: how long your savings can cover a monthly shortfall before something needs to change. Runway turns worry into a plan: "I am short 400 a month and have 40 months to work with" gives you a timescale for action.

Not all your savings are available to live on. Some will pay for the change, some will be tied up in deposits, and some will remain in your emergency reserve. Only what is left can cover a monthly shortfall. The calculation below shows how long it could last.

start_here.prompt: The middle column shows how it works, with made-up numbers. Write your own numbers in the last column.

fields.label: Question 1: every month

rows.label: 1. My confirmed income per month in my new life (from 3.4)
2. My costs per month in my new life (from 3.2)
3. Left over or short each month (1 minus 2)

fields.label: Question 2: my savings

rows.label: 4. Savings I can use within a month
5. Minus: the one-time cost of the change (from 3.3)
6. Minus: deposits, money I pay now and may only get back much later
7. Minus: my reserve, money I keep for emergencies and not to live on
8. Savings left to live on (4 minus 5, 6 and 7)

fields.label: Question 3: how long?
fields.hint: Only if you are short each month (line 3).

rows.label: 9. Months my savings can cover: line 8 divided by the amount I am short (line 3)

result_guide.title: What your result means
intro: Read these two checks separately.

Check one: can your savings cover the change itself? Look at line 8. Above zero means the one-time costs, deposits and reserve are covered, with money left to live on. Exactly zero means they are covered with nothing spare. Below zero means something needs to change: a cheaper version, a later date, a smaller reserve you deliberately choose, or more saving first.
Check two: does your confirmed income cover your monthly costs? That is line 3.
bullets: Money left over each month. The monthly side works on these numbers. Check one still decides whether you can afford to make the change at all.
Income and costs exactly equal. On these estimates, nothing is left over each month, so any surprise has to come out of your savings.

Short each month, with savings left. If these estimates hold, your remaining savings could cover the gap for about the number of months in line 9. Pick a date well before then to review the plan again.
Short each month, with no savings left to cover it. This version doesn't stand on its own yet. The three ways forward are lower costs, more confirmed income, or more time.

The amount you need is still unknown. Your result is incomplete, so do not treat the total as a finished calculation. Write what you need to check and where you will find the answer. That list is a useful result in its own right.
result_guide.closing: Do you plan to live on savings or a pension? Then look at how many years your money will last and discuss the plan with a financial adviser.

tips: The example is made up, but the costs are based on typical 2026 prices for a couple renting a small house in the interior of central Portugal (see the example in 3.2). The €6,000 reserve is made up too. Your reserve is yours to decide. A common way to think about it is how many months of costs you want covered if everything stopped. Do not know yet? Write a question mark and come back.
Short each month? That is not the end. It shows what to work on: lower costs, more income, or more time.

go_deeper.prompt: What if everything costs 30% more than you think? Does your plan still work? What would you change first: your costs, your income, or your timing?

story.text: A few years ago, I had savings in different accounts but no clear plan for them. The Perfect Life programme helped me set financial goals for the life I wanted. I could then see which investments to start and what budget I needed for my first house in Bali. I also set a monthly budget for my daily life and checked it every month. Before moving, I made sure I had twelve months of living costs saved. That gave me time to build my new life without the immediate pressure of running out of money and having to return. Knowing the numbers made the big decisions easier. My picture told me what I wanted; my plan showed me when I could afford it.

exercises.go_further: Want to go further? The module Your Money Plan (future) helps you with goals, a budget, investments and your "freedom date": the moment your investments could pay for your life.

summary.title: What does this tell me?
summary.intro: Read through your answers, then use these questions to complete the summary below:
questions: What do I know for sure?
What could change the picture a lot?
summary.prompt: Now bring it together in My First Money Picture. Short sentences are enough.

fields.label: What my new life costs per month, and how sure I am
What the change costs, one time
Income I can count on
Income I hope for
My first check: left over or short each month, and how many months my savings cover
My three words about money, and what they tell me
My biggest money unknowns, and how I will check them

summary.result: My First Money Picture — your first numbers, how sure they are, and what to check next.

parts.label: Part 4
parts.title: Compare your options
parts.promise: Moving far away is one option. It is not the only one.
parts.intro_title: Why we compare instead of decide
intro: You now have a picture of the life you want, an honest starting point, and a first money check. Before choosing a direction, put a few options side by side.
When we become attached to one option, it is easy to notice what supports it and explain away what does not. Keep at least three options open and compare them against the same list.

Always include two staying options. The first is to stay and change something important: you may be able to get much of what you want at a lower cost, while keeping the people and things that already work. The second is to change nothing. Include its costs too, so you can compare it fairly with making a change.
parts.talk: Find one person who made a change like the one you are thinking about: in the network, online, or through me. Ask: "What surprised you? What would you do differently?" One honest conversation can teach you a lot.

finish.title: My Options
finish.description: The options worth investigating, and what you need to learn about them.

exercises.title: Your options

start_here.prompt: Think of three or four options and write them down. Always include the two options about staying. For each promising option, write what you are not sure about, and a small test that could help you find out.

columns.label: What I am not sure about

example.text: A: Move with my family to the Algarve. Not sure: would working there feel good outside summer? Test: first, three calls with people who live there; then, if that holds up, a four-week working stay in November. C: Stay, but work four days a week. Not sure: can we live on less income? Test: live on 80% of our income for three months. D: Change nothing.

tips: A good test is small, cheap and quick, and it can prove you wrong. "Book a trip" is not a test. "Call three people who live there and ask what a Tuesday in February looks like" costs nothing and is a test. A four-week stay is a better test, but it's later and more expensive. Start with the cheap version.

exercises.title: Check your options against your must-haves
intro: Use the must-haves you identified in Part 1 to compare your options. Check whether each one meets those needs, regardless of how appealing it sounds.
Check the dealbreakers first. There is no need to score an option in detail if it already fails on something you will not accept.

start_here.prompt: First, check your dealbreakers (from 1.4). Does an option break one of them? Write which one. That option is out, unless you find a clear way around it.

fields.hint: Then check each must-have. For each option, mark it yes, partly, no or unknown. Unknown is a good answer before you have explored.
Then complete the overview. "My feeling" is how the option feels when you imagine it: 1 = bad, 5 = very good.

Ask two questions about staying. What would it protect: people, work, health, a home, a routine that works? And what would it cost in time, energy or happiness? Write down both to make the comparison fair.

tips: This comparison is not final. It does not choose a winner. It shows what you still need to find out, and that is where Step 2 begins.

summary.title: What does this tell me?
summary.intro: Read through your answers, then use these questions to complete the summary below:
questions: Which options do I still want to investigate?
What would each option need to work for me?
summary.prompt: Now bring it together in My Options. Short sentences are enough.

fields.label: Options I keep, and why
Options I let go, and why
What each option I keep would need to work for me
What worries me most, in one line
What I still need to find out

summary.closing: Step 3 looks at your worries properly, with a risk check for each option.
summary.result: My Options — the options worth investigating, and what you need to learn about them.

parts.label: Part 5
parts.title: Choose your working direction
parts.promise: Not a final decision. A clear next direction.
parts.intro_title: A direction is not a decision.
intro: You do not have to commit to a move here. A Working Direction says what you will explore next and what you need to learn before deciding. Change it when what you learn points you elsewhere.

Make your next step specific. It should be small enough to complete within two weeks, have a date, and teach you something. "Read more about Portugal" gives you no clear question or deadline. "Call two people who moved there and ask what surprised them, before the 15th" gives you both.
The last line looks two years ahead. How will you know this has worked? Describe it through the ordinary days you wrote about earlier. You will return to this answer in Step 8.
The final decision comes in Step 3, after you have explored your options.
parts.talk: Tell one person about your working direction this week. Saying it out loud makes it more real. Are other people moving with you? Ask each of them to fill in their own page first. Then sit together and compare.

finish.title: My Working Direction
finish.description: What you want to explore, what you take with you, and your next step.

exercises.title: My Working Direction

fields.label: My life picture in three sentences
What I choose now
options: Build the life I want where I am

fields.label: The direction(s) I want to explore
Why: two or three reasons
My essential needs: I take these with me
Assumptions I still need to check
What I need to learn next
What I am willing to invest: time, money, comfort
Who can help me
The first question I will investigate, and why it matters most
My next small step, within two weeks
What this step will help me learn
Date of this step
When I will review what I learned
What result would make me continue, change direction, or stop
In two years, how I will know this worked

exercises.choice_explanations_intro: For "What I choose now", five answers are possible, and all five are good:
choice_explanations: I have a direction I want to investigate. Step 2 is waiting for you.
I want to compare two or more directions. Step 2 helps you explore them side by side.
I want to build the life I want where I am. Staying is a real result. It takes the same work of deciding, planning and building. We are developing a full staying route with the first participants.
I am not ready to choose yet. Your page shows what you need to learn first.

I want to keep the life I have. You may find that your life already fits. Write down what you want to protect, and leave the questions about change blank where they do not apply. Keeping a good life is a decision too.

example.text: What I choose now: not ready yet. While doing this workbook, my wife and I found out that we want different things. She wants to stay close to our grandchildren. I want to live by the sea. We will each write our own normal day first, then talk about what we both need. That feels like progress, even without a decision.

example_page.title: A completed page
example_page.intro: Rosa is made up, and she ends up staying. The point is not her answer. It is that every line is filled in, including the parts she does not know yet.
rows: My life picture in three sentences
I want time outside every day. I want work I choose, not work that fills every hour. I want my parents close enough to visit in an afternoon.
Build the life I want where I am.
The direction(s) I want to explore
Four days a week instead of five, in my current job, and one day a week outside.

My parents are twenty minutes away, and that is worth more to me than better weather. Most of what I wanted from moving was time, not another country. A colleague already works four days, so it is possible here.
My essential needs: I take these with me
Daily time outside. Work I choose. No commute over 30 minutes.
Assumptions I still need to check
That we can live on about 80% of my income. That my manager will agree in writing. That one day less does not become five days of work in four.
What I need to learn next
What a year on 80% really costs us, using our own numbers.
What I am willing to invest: time, money, comfort
About 20% of my income, and one uncomfortable conversation at work.
My partner, for the budget. My colleague who already works four days.
The first question I will investigate, and why it matters most
Can we live on 80%? If the answer is no, the rest does not matter, whatever my manager says.
My next small step, within two weeks
Redo Part 3 with 80% of my take-home pay, using our last three bank statements.
What this step will help me learn
Whether the gap is small enough to close by cutting costs, or big enough to need another plan.
When I will review what I learned
1 November, whatever has happened by then.
What result would make me continue, change direction, or stop
A gap under 150 a month: continue, and ask my manager. A bigger gap: look at other work here first, before I reopen the idea of moving.
In two years, how I will know this worked
I am outside every day, not only at weekends. I see my parents every week. And my Fridays are still mine.

exercises.title: The people involved
intro: If you are making this choice with someone else, fill in the table together after each of you has worked through your own answers. I have seen how easily a conversation can end with one person's picture and the other person simply agreeing to it.

story.text: When I first described the life I wanted, I did not know many of the details. I had no plan for an inspection business, but I knew I loved building. I had not imagined writing this Blueprint, but I knew I was good at helping and supporting people. The details took shape as I went. Start with what you know now and take a first step. You will learn more by doing it.

parts.result: My Working Direction — what you want to explore, what you take with you, and your next step.

closing.title: What comes next
closing.intro: You have made your picture clearer, looked honestly at your life and your money, and chosen a Working Direction.
bullets: Want to investigate a direction? Step 2, Explore, helps you check it. The questions work for Portugal and for other places.

Building the life you want where you are? Choose one change from your staying option. Write what you will change in the next three months, and how you will notice if it helps. Talk it through with the people it affects. Until the full staying route is ready, your Working Direction is your guide.
Not ready yet? Your page tells you what to learn first.
tips: Read this workbook again in a few months. See what changed, what didn't, and what you want to try next.
final: You cannot control everything. But you can choose, prepare, and take the next step.
You just took the first one.

sources.title: Where these ideas come from
sources.intro: Most of this workbook comes from my experience of building a life in Bali and then starting again in Portugal. Where I draw on someone else's method, I name it below.
rows: A tool used in coaching for decades, with no single owner. I first used it myself during my year in Bali, and I still do it every year.
Described by the psychologists Joseph Luft and Harrington Ingham in the 1950s. The part I use here is the simple idea that other people can see things about you that you cannot see yourself.

Several questions draw on Michael Pilarczyk's programmes, which I followed myself. They include the two-million question that helped me plan my own move. I have adapted the wording for this Blueprint.
The phrase comes from Steve Jobs' 2005 speech at Stanford University.
Common practice in planning and decision-making. Bill Burnett and Dave Evans describe similar ideas in their book Designing Your Life.
My own experience, my mistakes, and what the people I have guided told me was missing.
sources.closing: Rules, prices and official procedures change, so this workbook does not state any. You will find those, with their sources and dates, in Step 2 and Step 3, where they belong.
